title: Mapping Marriage in America: Where Young Adults Marry Most | Institute for Family Studies
gist: IFS's 'Mapping Marriage in America' report (built from 2020-2024 ACS/IPUMS microdata at the PUMA level) finds that the best marriage markets flip by age — rural/interior areas favor marriage in one's 20s while superstar cities (San Jose, LA, NY, Chicago) favor marriage in one's 30s — and that the ratio of employed and higher-earning single men to single women, not raw population density, religiosity, or urbanicity, is the strongest predictor of local marriage rates, with the income and education effects reversing sign between the 20s and 30s.

insights.claim: The Provo, Utah region has the nation's highest overall marriage rate among adults ages 22-39 (13.2%), with five other top-10 regions clustered in a band between Panama City, FL and Fort Wayne, IN, and additional strength in the northern Dallas-Fort Worth suburbs.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel, Wendy Wang and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Establishes Provo as the clear national outlier for marriage formation and identifies a specific Panama City-to-Fort Wayne 'marriage belt' as a durable regional pattern worth tracking for family-formation-linked demand (housing, childcare, family services).
insights.quote: The Provo, Utah, region is the highest-ranking area on this list with a marriage rate of 13.2%.
insights.locator: section 'Where Are Marriage Rates the Highest?'

insights.claim: For adults ages 22-29, marriage rates are highest in interior states (Utah, Kansas, Nebraska, Tennessee, Kentucky) and lowest in eight of the ten worst regions, which are located in the Los Angeles and New York metropolitan areas.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel, Wendy Wang and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Young adults who want to marry in their 20s should be cautious about relocating to LA or NYC, where the local marriage market for that age group is structurally weak regardless of dating-app density or population size.
insights.quote: eight of the 10 regions with the lowest marriage rates among adults ages 22-29 are located in the Los Angeles and New York metropolitan areas ... this finding suggests that those who desire to get married at a younger age might want to think carefully before moving to these regions
insights.locator: section on lowest marriage rates ages 22-29

insights.claim: The pattern reverses for adults ages 30-39: the highest marriage rates for this group cluster near major cities — San Jose, Los Angeles, New York, and Chicago — plus strength in Austin, Nashville, Pittsburgh, and Boston, while Colorado is also a notable hotspot despite not appearing in the strict top 10.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel, Wendy Wang and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Superstar cities that suppress marriage in the 20s become strong marriage markets in the 30s, implying many residents delay rather than forgo marriage — relevant to timing assumptions in household-formation and housing-demand models tied to these metros.
insights.quote: The 10 regions with the highest marriage rates among adults in this age group, unlike those in the top 10 for adults ages 22-29, tend to be located near major cities; examples include San Jose, Los Angeles, New York, and Chicago.
insights.locator: section on highest marriage rates ages 30-39

insights.claim: The Fort Wayne/Southern Suburbs region of Indiana is the only region that appears in both the top-10 marriage-rate lists for the 22-29 and 30-39 age groups.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel, Wendy Wang and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Flags Fort Wayne as a uniquely age-agnostic strong marriage market, a potential outlier case study for what drives consistent (not just age-skewed) family formation.
insights.quote: Only one region appears within both this top-10 list and the list for adults ages 22-29: the Fort Wayne/Southern Suburbs region of Indiana.
insights.locator: section on highest marriage rates ages 30-39

insights.claim: The lowest marriage rates for adults ages 22-39 overall are concentrated in the Mississippi Delta, New Mexico, and southwestern Georgia; for the 30-39 age group specifically, weak markets also appear in the Southwestern U.S., western South Carolina, western Pennsylvania, and parts of the DC, Chicago, and Phoenix metro areas.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel, Wendy Wang and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Maps a persistent geography of weak marriage markets across age groups, largely overlapping economically distressed regions — relevant for targeting family-policy interventions.
insights.quote: Marriage rates for this age group also tend to be lower within the Mississippi Delta, New Mexico, and southwestern Georgia.
insights.locator: section on lowest marriage rates overall

themes.theme: Employment and earnings ratios drive marriage rates, not raw singles population

insights.claim: A substantial positive correlation exists between an area's marriage rate for young-adult women and the percentage of women in that age group who are already married — meaning areas with more singles are actually worse marriage markets, not better, contrary to intuition.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel, Wendy Wang and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Directly refutes the common assumption that 'more singles nearby = better odds of marrying' — a key reframe for anyone using local singles density as a proxy for marriage-market quality.
insights.quote: while one might think that areas where more individuals are single are better places to find a spouse, the opposite is actually true
insights.locator: section 'Which Metrics Correlate With Getting Married?'

insights.claim: The ratio of single, full-time-employed men to all single women is a strong predictor of women's marriage rates across ages 22-39, and to a lesser extent predicts men's marriage rates as well.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel, Wendy Wang and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Establishes the single best available metric (employed men per 100 single women) for screening geographic marriage-market quality, more predictive than density, religiosity, or politics.
insights.quote: Among women ages 22-39, the ratio of single, full-time-employed men to all single women has a strong connection with marriage rates.
insights.locator: section 'Availability of employed single men helps predict marriage rates'

insights.claim: Regions with the highest ratio of single, full-time-employed men to single women are dominated by military bases (Minot, ND; Fayetteville and Jacksonville, NC; Oceanside/Camp Pendleton, CA; El Paso Teller near Colorado Springs, CO; the Peninsula Region/JBLM, WA) as well as tech hubs like Mountain View and Sunnyvale, CA.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel, Wendy Wang and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Identifies two structurally distinct 'good marriage market' archetypes for women — military-installation towns and big-tech employment hubs — both driven by male-skewed local labor markets.
insights.quote: Many of the regions with the highest score for this metric are located in areas with a large military presence ... Mountain View and Sunnyvale, CA also have notably high ratios of single, full-time employed men to single women, likely due, in part, to the large presence of major tech companies
insights.locator: section on highest employed-men ratios

insights.claim: The lowest ratios of employed single men to single women are found mostly in Midwestern cities, the Bronx, and the South, with Fresno and Baltimore also in the bottom 10, plus much of Mississippi, Alabama, parts of the NYC area, and southern Virginia.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel, Wendy Wang and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Maps out the structurally weakest marriage markets by employment-ratio, a distinct and complementary geography to the overall lowest-marriage-rate list.
insights.quote: The 10 areas with the lowest ratios, in contrast, are mostly found within Midwestern cities, the Bronx, and the South.
insights.locator: section on lowest employed-men ratios

themes.theme: Income and education effects reverse sign between the 20s and 30s (ecological-fallacy risk)

insights.claim: Only 32% of single men ages 30-39 and 19% of single men ages 22-29 have personal incomes of $60,000 or more (a 'good wage' benchmark from the Good Jobs, Strong Families report by Grant Martsolf and Brad Wilcox); the corresponding shares for single women are slightly lower — 27% (30-39) and 15% (22-29).
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel, Wendy Wang and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Quantifies how small the pool of $60k+ earners is among young singles — under a fifth of single men in their 20s — a hard constraint on the 'higher-earning spouse' supply in most local marriage markets.
insights.quote: we found that only 32% of single men ages 30-39, and 19% of single men ages 22-29, have personal incomes of $60,000 or more
insights.locator: section 'Women's marriage rates and the availability of higher-earning single men'

insights.claim: The regional ratio of single men earning $60,000+ to single women has a strong positive correlation with women's marriage rates in their 30s, but essentially no correlation with women's marriage rates in their 20s.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel, Wendy Wang and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Regional income screening for marriageability sharply diverges by age — men's high earnings matter for regional marriage-market dynamics mainly once women are in their 30s, not their 20s.
insights.quote: the relative availability of higher-earning men has a strong connection to marriage rates for women in their thirties, but not for this younger group
insights.locator: section on age divergence in income effect

insights.claim: Seven of the top 10 regions for the ratio of $60k+ single men to single women are in Seattle, San Jose, and San Francisco (major tech hubs); the remaining three are in the New York or Washington, DC metro areas; nationally, high values also appear along the Washington-Boston corridor and in Austin, Minneapolis, and Colorado.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel, Wendy Wang and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Confirms tech-hub and Northeast-corridor metros as the primary geography of high-earning single male density, the labor-market backdrop shaping marriage markets for women in their 30s in those cities.
insights.quote: Seven of the top 10 regions for this ratio are located in Seattle, San Jose, and San Francisco—all major tech hubs with plenty of highly-paid employees.
insights.locator: section on highest $60k+ men ratios

insights.claim: The lowest ratios of $60k+ single men to single women are concentrated in rural areas of the Southeast and Appalachia, and outside major metros like Atlanta and Raleigh the broader Southeastern U.S. tends to score low on this metric.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel, Wendy Wang and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Identifies rural Southeast/Appalachia as structurally weak on high-earning male supply, compounding other regional disadvantages (job availability, wages) already known in these areas.
insights.quote: the 10 regions with the lowest ratios tend to be located in more rural areas of the Southeast and Appalachia
insights.locator: section on lowest $60k+ men ratios

insights.claim: At the regional level, the share of single men in their 30s with a bachelor's degree positively correlates with that group's marriage rate, but among single men in their 20s the correlation is small and negative — likely because degree-holders concentrate in large cities where 20s marriage rates are structurally lower.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel, Wendy Wang and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: A regional-education 'sign flip' by age that could mislead simplistic models linking education concentration to marriage outcomes if age cohorts aren't separated.
insights.quote: among single men ages 22-29, the percentage of men with BAs has a much smaller, and negative, correlation with marriage rates. This may be because men with a bachelor's degree are more likely to live in large cities than those without one.
insights.locator: section 'For men, regional relationship between education and marriage is also age dependent'

insights.claim: Despite the regional-level sign flip, within every age group individual men and women with a bachelor's degree have higher marriage rates than those without one, and men ages 22-29 earning at least $60,000 are about twice as likely to marry in a given year as those earning less — the regional correlation reversal does not hold at the individual level.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel, Wendy Wang and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: A textbook ecological-fallacy warning: regional aggregate correlations between income/education and marriage can run opposite to individual-level effects, so policymakers and researchers should not infer individual-level causal effects from regional data in this domain.
insights.quote: men ages 22-29 who earn at least $60,000 are around twice as likely to get married in a given year as those who do not ... moving to a region with lots of higher-earning young men will not necessarily result in better odds of marriage
insights.locator: section 'Regional relationship between higher incomes and marriage differs by age for men'

themes.theme: Politics and religion don't map cleanly onto marriage geography

insights.claim: Trump's 2024 vote margin over Harris is positively and relatively strongly correlated with marriage rates for both men and women ages 22-29, but the relationship is much weaker and negatively correlated for adults in their 30s — likely because more rural, Trump-favoring areas tend to have higher marriage rates specifically among 20-somethings.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel, Wendy Wang and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Political geography (2024 election results) tracks marriage-rate geography for young adults, but the relationship is age-dependent and should not be read as a simple 'red areas marry more' rule across all ages.
insights.quote: These two variables have a positive and relatively strong correlation for men and women ages 22-29; however, for thirty-something adults of each sex, this relationship is much weaker and negatively correlated.
insights.locator: section 'Religion, Ideology, and Marriage Rates'

insights.claim: Despite General Social Survey data showing that religious individuals in their 20s and 30s are significantly more likely to be married than nominal/secular peers, the report finds essentially no regional correlation between an area's religious-adherent share and its young-adult marriage rate.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel, Wendy Wang and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: A striking individual-vs-ecological divergence: religiosity predicts marriage strongly at the person level but not at the regional level, so 'move to a religious area to find a spouse' is not supported by this regional data even though 'be religious yourself' is.
insights.quote: we find essentially no regional relationship between religious-adherent shares and the percentage of young adults who got married in the past year
insights.locator: section on religion and marriage rates

insights.claim: The report is built on 2020-2024 IPUMS American Community Survey microdata at the Public Use Microdata Area (PUMA) level, with marriage-rate calculations grouped into PUMA clusters of at least 500,000 people; county-level religious-adherence and 2024 election data were converted to estimated PUMA-level figures, a process the authors flag as having significant limitations for partial-county PUMAs.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel, Wendy Wang and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Analysts using this report's religion/politics correlations should apply extra caution given the acknowledged county-to-PUMA conversion error, more so than for the core employment/marriage-rate findings.
insights.quote: Because our election-result data, as well as our religious-adherent data, was originally provided at the county level, we needed to convert it into estimated PUMA-level data ... this approach has some significant limitations
insights.locator: endnotes

insights.claim: Marriage rates are measured by current residence, not residence at time of marriage, which can bias results in areas with heavy post-marriage relocation; in the San Jose area, women's ages 30-39 marriage rate drops from 14.2% to 10.9% when recent movers are excluded, suggesting a meaningful share of women relocate to San Jose specifically to live with new husbands working in tech.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel, Wendy Wang and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: A concrete magnitude (roughly a 3.3-point rate inflation) for how much migration-for-marriage can distort a hot labor-market metro's apparent marriage rate — relevant for adjusting any market that draws in-migration tied to high-earning male employment.
insights.quote: 14.2% of never-married women ages 30-39 in San Jose got married in the past year; however, when we exclude women who changed migration PUMAs during that time, this value drops to 10.9%
insights.locator: endnote 4 on San Jose migration bias

insights.claim: The average grouped-PUMA-level marriage rate across the study period was 6.6% for women ages 22-39 versus 5.5% for men, a persistent gender gap in the measured annual marriage rate.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel, Wendy Wang and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: A baseline gender asymmetry in measured marriage rates (driven by denominator/age-range mismatches, per the authors) that should be accounted for when comparing male vs. female marriage-rate maps.
insights.quote: The average grouped-PUMA-level marriage rate for women ages 22-39 was 6.6, a decent amount higher than the average for men (5.5).
insights.locator: endnotes

insights.claim: The authors plan to continue updating the Get Married Maps (GoGetMarried.org) as new demographic data becomes available, framing today's top marriage regions as potentially subject to change.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel, Wendy Wang and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Signals this data series will be refreshed periodically, making it a trackable recurring indicator of regional family-formation trends rather than a one-off snapshot.
insights.quote: we plan to continue updating these maps as new demographic data becomes available
insights.locator: conclusion
